Small, medium and large jobs

Think of jobs by **size and risk**, not just by money. A small job is a home birthday with one balloon garland, a backdrop and a cake table, set up in two to three hours by you and one helper. A medium job is a 100 to 200 guest party or church reception with tablecloths, centrepieces, a backdrop and an entrance, needing four to six hours and two or three helpers. A large job is a wedding reception for several hundred guests with ceiling draping, a stage, lighting and many tables, often needing a crew and a setup that starts the night before.

Start where a mistake is survivable. If a balloon garland at a home birthday comes out uneven, you can fix it in twenty minutes. If you misjudge the setup time for a 400 guest wedding, there is no fixing it once the couple arrives. Most successful decorators grow by doing many small jobs very well, collecting photos and referrals, and only then taking on bigger halls.

The difference between decor that looks expensive and decor that looks busy is rarely money. It is usually **colour control** and **one clear focal point**. A hall with three well-chosen colours, repeated everywhere, looks planned. A hall with seven colours scattered around looks confused, even if each item is beautiful.

Three colour schemes every decorator uses

A **colour wheel** arranges colours in a circle: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, purple, and the shades between them. You can find free colour wheel tools on your phone, such as Adobe Color in the browser. Three simple schemes cover most events.
Scheme
How to build it
Event example
Monochrome
One colour in light, medium and dark shades, plus white or a neutral
Blush, rose and deep pink with white for a girl's birthday

Two or three colours sitting next to each other on the wheel

Metallics such as gold, silver and rose gold behave like neutrals. They sit happily with most schemes and add shine under lights. White, ivory and cream also act as calm backgrounds that let your main colours stand out.
The 60-30-10 rule

Interior designers use a simple proportion guide called the **60-30-10 rule**: about 60 percent of what the eye sees is the main colour, about 30 percent is a second colour, and about 10 percent is an accent. It is a guide, not a law, but it stops a room from looking evenly split and flat.
60-30-10 colour balance
10% accent: gold details
30% secondary: champagne fabric
60% main: white base
The biggest surfaces carry the main colour; small details carry the accent.

In a hall the big surfaces are tablecloths, chair covers, wall or ceiling drapes and the backdrop. These carry your 60 percent. Table runners, chair sashes and balloon clusters often carry the 30 percent. Napkin rings, candle holders, flowers and small props carry the 10 percent accent.
One focal point, supported

Every room needs one place where eyes go first. At a wedding reception it is usually the high table and backdrop. At a birthday it is the cake table with its balloon garland. At a church event it is the altar or stage. Spend the largest share of your effort and budget there, keep the guest tables simpler, and use the entrance to give guests a first taste of the colours.
Aso ebi comes first

At many Nigerian weddings the families choose aso ebi colours early. Ask for photos of the actual fabric, not just the colour name, because "wine" or "champagne" can mean very different shades. Build your palette to sit well with the fabric guests will wear, so photos look unified.

Height, texture and repetition

Colour is only half of design. A table where every item is the same height looks flat, so mix one tall element (a candle stand or a tall vase), some medium pieces and some low ones. Mix textures too: shiny satin next to soft chiffon, matte balloons next to chrome ones, fresh leaves next to glass. Finally, **repeat** your key elements. The same flower or balloon cluster appearing at the entrance, the backdrop and the cake table ties the whole room together, and guests feel it even if they cannot say why.

Keep sightlines open on guest tables. Centrepieces should be either low, below about chin height when seated, or tall and slim so guests can talk across the table under them. A wide, medium-height arrangement blocks faces and usually gets moved to the floor by guests within an hour.

Always check colours in the light of the venue. A balloon that looks peach in daylight can look orange under warm hall bulbs. When you can, take a sample balloon or fabric swatch to the venue and look at it where it will hang.

Core safety rules you will follow at every job
Decoration puts open flames, electricity, ladders and lots of flammable fabric in rooms full of people. Learn these rules now and treat them as non-negotiable.
Safety before guests arrive
Candles 12 inches from fabric
No overloaded extension boxes
Cables taped flat, away from water
Ladder held by a helper
Exits and walkways kept clear
Heavy pieces weighted or tied
Walk the room with this checklist before you hand over to the client.

**Candles:** The US Fire Administration advises keeping candles at least 12 inches (about 30 cm) from anything that can burn, in stable holders where they cannot be knocked over. Near drapes, flowers or balloons, use battery-operated flameless candles instead.
**Electrics:** Do not plug one extension box into another. Keep cables taped down where people walk, away from drinks and water, and switch off lights you are adjusting.
**Generators:** Generators produce carbon monoxide, a poisonous gas you cannot smell. They must run outside, never inside a hall, canopy or closed room.
**Heights:** Use a proper step ladder, never a stacked chair, and have a helper hold it.
**Weight:** Backdrop stands and balloon arches catch wind outdoors. Weight their bases with sandbags or water weights and tie them to fixed points.

Fabric deserves special attention. Light materials such as chiffon, voile and organza catch fire easily and burn fast. Keep them well away from candles, hot halogen bulbs and generator exhausts, and never drape fabric directly over a hot light fitting. Ask your fabric supplier whether a material is flame-retardant; if they cannot say, treat it as flammable.
Know where the fire extinguisher is
At every venue, find the fire extinguisher and the exits before you start. If the venue has none, bring a small fire extinguisher whenever your design uses real candles or many electrical lights.

Most decoration disputes start with words that meant different things to the client and the decorator: "elegant", "not too much", "gold". A **client brief** is a short, structured conversation that turns those words into specific decisions you both agree on. It protects your time, the client's money and your reputation.
Two people having a conversation
A good brief is a conversation with written answers, not a quick chat you try to remember later.
The brief questions
Ask these questions in person, on a call or by WhatsApp voice note, then send a written summary back so the client can confirm it. Keep the list in your phone and use it every time.
**The event:** type, date, start time, end time, and the time guests start arriving.
**The venue:** exact address, indoor or outdoor, contact person at the venue, earliest time you can enter, and when you must clear out.
**Guests:** expected number, and how many tables and what shape (round or rectangular).
**Look:** colours (with aso ebi or fabric photos), theme, three pictures they love and one they dislike.
**Zones:** which areas they want decorated: entrance, backdrop, stage or high table, guest tables, cake table, ceiling.
**Budget:** a range for decoration only, not the whole event.
**Rules:** anything the venue or church does not allow, such as nails, tape on walls, open flames or confetti.
Ask for one picture they dislike
Clients often struggle to explain what they want, but they know immediately what they do not want. One disliked picture can save you from a whole wrong direction.
The venue check

Visit the venue if you can, or ask the client or venue manager for a slow walk-through video. Measure with a tape measure and write numbers down. You need: the room length and width, the ceiling height, the backdrop wall width, the size and position of the stage, the number and size of tables, door widths for carrying in large pieces, and the location of power sockets. Note the light: warm yellow bulbs, white fluorescent tubes or daylight all change how colours look.

Photograph each wall and corner, the ceiling and any fixed hooks or beams. Ask the venue manager who supplies chairs and tables, whether they provide covers, whether there is a generator and who runs it, and whether another event is booked in the hall before yours. A morning wedding in the same hall can cut your setup window in half.

The design proposal

Keep the proposal to one or two pages so it is easy to read on a phone. Include a **mood board** (six to nine photos showing the colours and style), a simple **sketch** of the main focal point with measurements, a **zone list** describing each area in one line, and the **quotation** (covered in lesson 3 of this module). Clients see the finished room; your skill is in the building. This lesson covers the four pieces that appear at almost every Nigerian event: balloon work, backdrops, fabric draping and table settings. Practise each at home before using it on a paid job.
A single red balloon
Balloon work is often the first thing guests photograph, so even sizing matters.
Balloon garlands and arches

Latex balloons are commonly sold in sizes such as 5 inch, 11 inch and 18 inch. An **organic garland** mixes these sizes for a natural, cloud-like look. A **classic arch** uses clusters of balloons of one size in a regular pattern on a frame. For most beginners the organic garland is easier and more forgiving.
Inflate 11 inch balloons slightly under full size so they are rounder and less likely to burst. Use a sizer so they match.
Inflate a smaller number of 18 inch balloons for volume and many 5 inch balloons for filling gaps.
Tie two balloons together by their necks to make a pair, then twist two pairs together to make a cluster of four.
Push the knots through the holes of a balloon decorating strip, or twist clusters onto a strong line, rotating each cluster so the garland is round.
Attach the garland to the backdrop stand or frame with cable ties or fishing line, then add 18 inch and 5 inch balloons with glue dots to fill gaps.
Count by test-building

Do not guess balloon numbers. Build 30 cm (one foot) of garland in your chosen style, count the balloons, then multiply by the total length you need and add about 10 percent for bursts. Record the count for future quotes.

Air-filled garlands last much longer than helium balloons, which lose float within hours to a day. Sunlight makes latex cloudy and weak, so keep outdoor balloon work in shade where possible and set it up close to the event time. Some guests are allergic to latex; for an indoor event with a known allergy, use foil balloons and fabric instead. Keep foil balloons away from overhead power lines, as the metallic coating can conduct electricity.
Backdrops and fabric draping

A backdrop is usually an adjustable pipe frame with fabric panels hung from the top bar. To look full rather than flat, fabric needs **gathers**. Decorators commonly use 1.5 to 2 times the frame width in fabric. For a 3 m wide frame, that means about 4.5 m to 6 m of total fabric width. Satin gives shine, chiffon and voile give soft, see-through layers, and many decorators layer a solid fabric behind a sheer one.

Draping ceilings or walls needs secure anchor points and the venue's permission. Never hang fabric from light fittings, fans or electrical cables. If the hall has no safe fixing points, use free-standing frames instead.
Table settings

Tablecloth size comes from simple maths: **cloth diameter = table diameter + 2 × drop**. The drop is how far the cloth hangs down each side. A standard dining table is about 30 inches (76 cm) high, so a 30 inch drop reaches the floor.

Many decorators work hard and still lose money because they price by feeling or by copying others. A **quotation** is a written price that lists what you will provide, what it costs and the terms of payment. Built properly, it covers every naira you spend, pays you for your time and leaves profit to grow the business.
A paper receipt
A clear, itemised quotation prevents arguments about what was included.
The six parts of a quotation
**Materials you use up:** balloons, flowers, glue dots, tape, printed signs.
**Rentals:** cloths, chair covers, frames, stands, lights.
**Wear on your own items:** a small charge for things you own, so you can replace them.
**Labour:** you and your helpers, including setup and pack-down hours.
**Transport:** trips to market, to the venue and back, and any delivery fees.
**Contingency and profit:** a buffer for price changes and breakages, then your profit margin.

Deposits and payment terms

Never buy or rent for a client without a deposit. The deposit covers what you must spend in advance and shows the client is committed. Many decorators ask for a large part upfront, for example 50 to 70 percent on approval, with the balance paid a few days before the event, not after it. Write your terms on the quotation: deposit amount, balance due date, what happens if the client cancels (for example, the deposit covers costs already spent), and how many days the quotation is valid, since market prices change. Send a short receipt or acknowledgement message for every payment you receive, showing the amount, the date and the balance still due.
Payment scams

Only accept a payment as received when it shows in your bank or wallet app, such as Opay or Moniepoint. Screenshots of "successful" transfers can be faked. A payment link from Paystack or your bank also gives the client a clear receipt.
Rent or buy?

Buy an item only when renting it repeatedly would cost more. Divide the purchase price by what you pay to rent it each time. The answer is the number of uses to **break even**. Also consider storage space, cleaning and transport: a stack of 100 chair covers needs washing, ironing and dry storage.

On the event day you are racing a clock you do not control. Guests arrive when the invitation says, not when you finish. Good decorators plan the day **backwards**: start with the moment the room must be ready, then subtract each task, travel time and a buffer, until you reach the time you must leave home.

List every setup task with a time estimate from your practice sessions, such as tables, backdrop, balloon garland, entrance and cake table.
Decide which tasks run in parallel, with different crew members working at the same time.

Packing and loading

Pack by **zone**, not by item type. Put everything for the cake table in one crate labelled "Cake table", everything for the backdrop in another, and keep a separate "tools" crate with scissors, tape, cable ties, glue dots, pins, flameless candles with spare batteries, extension box and a small first aid kit. Tick each crate off a packing list as it goes into the vehicle, and again when it comes out. Load the items you need first last, so they come out first.
Inflate early, but not too early
Air-filled garlands can often be built the evening before and transported in large bags. Helium balloons should be inflated as close to the event as possible, because they lose float within hours.
Crew roles

Give each helper a clear job and a photo of what the finished zone should look like. One person leads tables, one leads the backdrop, and you move between zones checking quality and solving problems. Avoid having everyone wait for you to give instructions; that wastes the most valuable hour of the morning.

Agree helpers' pay, arrival time and food before the day, and share the run sheet with them on WhatsApp the evening before. Confirm deliveries the day before too: call the rental company to confirm the number of cloths and chair covers, the delivery time and the exact address. Save the venue contact's number and the client's agreed contact person in your phone, because the bride or celebrant should not be the one answering decoration questions on the morning of her event.

Keep a small **emergency kit** in your tools crate: spare balloons in every colour you are using, extra cable ties, a second roll of tape, safety pins, a needle and thread, a small steamer or travel iron if the venue has power, and a phone power bank. Most morning crises are solved by one of these items.
The final walkthrough standard
**Matches the approval:** colours, zones and focal point are what the client approved.
**Secure:** stands weighted, garlands tied, nothing leaning; give each piece a gentle shake.
**Safe:** walkways and exits clear, cables taped, candles flameless or safely spaced.
**Neat:** equal tablecloth drops, no creases, no visible tape or ties, no balloon scraps on the floor.
**Clean:** packaging, offcuts and empty bags removed from the hall.

Take photos of every zone before guests arrive, while the room is empty and tidy. These become your portfolio pictures and your proof of what you delivered. Then hand over to the client or venue contact and tell them who to call if something needs attention during the event.

Outdoor events

Many Nigerian events happen under canopies on compounds or in gardens. Wind is the main enemy. Weight every stand with sandbags or water weights, tie arches to fixed posts or stakes, and avoid large flat panels that act like sails. Keep balloons in shade where you can, since direct sun weakens latex and makes it cloudy. In the rainy season, ask the client about tents and keep fabrics and electrics well clear of rainwater runoff.
Children at the party
At children's events, keep small burst balloon pieces off the floor, since they are a choking hazard for young children. Pick up bursts immediately and keep uninflated balloons out of reach.
Honest dealing

Things change between quotation and event day: a flower is out of season, a rental company runs out of gold chairs, a fabric colour arrives slightly different. Tell the client as soon as you know, explain the option you recommend and any price difference, and get agreement in writing. A silent substitution, discovered on the day, damages trust more than the change itself.

Be honest about capacity too. If you are offered two events on the same Saturday and your crew can only handle one properly, decline the second or refer it to a decorator you trust. A client's wedding happens once; doing it badly because you overbooked is not recoverable.

Honesty also covers your marketing. Only post photos of work you actually did, and say clearly when a picture is inspiration rather than your own setup. If you worked as part of another decorator's crew, credit them. Clients who book you because of borrowed photos will be disappointed on the day, and in a city where vendors talk to each other, that story travels quickly.
Common event-day problems
**Hall still in use:** confirm the handover time in writing the day before and plan a shorter setup with more helpers if needed.
**Late rental delivery:** start with zones that use your own items, such as the backdrop and balloons, while you chase the delivery.
**Balloons bursting in heat:** under-inflate slightly, keep spares, and keep balloons away from direct sun and hot lights.
Worked example: a problem on the day
For example, Amaka in Abuja arrives at a hotel for a 4 pm wedding reception and finds the hall's ceiling hooks, which she planned to use for draping, have been removed during renovations.
She stops and checks the time: setup started at 9:00, ready time is 3:00, so she has six hours.
She drops the ceiling drape, which needs safe anchor points, rather than improvising from light fittings.
She moves the drape fabric to two extra backdrop frames placed either side of the high table, making the focal point wider and fuller.
She calls the bride's sister, the agreed contact, explains the change and the reason, and offers a partial refund for the ceiling draping as listed on the quotation.
She notes in her records to confirm fixing points again 48 hours before every future ceiling job.
The room is safe, the focal point is stronger, the client heard about the change before seeing it, and Amaka keeps both her reputation and the referral.

After the event, pack down as carefully as you set up. Remove every cable tie, clip and piece of tape, return the venue to the condition you found it, and count rented items against your rental list so nothing is lost or charged to you.

Each event is a lesson you have already paid for. Without records, the lesson disappears after the weekend. With a simple job record, you learn how long things really take, what each event really costs and which clients send you more work.
A person giving feedback with stars and comments
Short, specific client feedback is the raw material for better jobs and stronger marketing.
Asking for feedback

Send a short message one or two days after the event, when the client has rested but still remembers. Ask specific questions rather than "how was it?". Clients answer more honestly when questions are easy and specific.
On a scale of 1 to 5, how close was the decor to what you pictured?
Was anything not as you expected, on the day or in our communication?
Did guests comment on any part of the decor?
May I share photos of the decor (without your guests' faces) and a sentence from your message on my page?
Would you recommend me to a friend? Who might need a decorator soon?
Privacy and permission

Ask before posting photos that show the client, their family or guests, especially children. Many decorators photograph the room before guests arrive so they can share decor freely without showing people.

Treat negative feedback as useful information, not an attack. Thank the client, ask one follow-up question to understand exactly what went wrong, and reply with what you will change. If a mistake was clearly yours, such as a missing item that was on the quotation, offer a fair remedy. A calm, honest reply often turns an unhappy client into one who still recommends you because of how you handled it.

Watch the room during the event too, if you are staying or can return. Notice which zones guests photograph most, whether centrepieces were moved because they blocked views, and whether anything sagged or fell as the hall warmed up. These observations are often more honest than anything a polite client will tell you afterwards.
The job record

Keep one row per job in a notebook or a free spreadsheet such as Google Sheets. Record the date, event type, guest count, quoted price, actual costs, setup time planned and actual, crew size, client rating and whether a referral came from it. Add one line on what to do differently next time.

For example, Tolu reviews her last three birthday jobs in Lagos (amounts approximate).

Job 2: quoted ₦190,000, actual costs ₦176,000, profit ₦14,000. Fresh flower prices rose after she quoted. Setup 3 hours, actual 3 hours 30 minutes.
Job 3: quoted ₦350,000, actual costs ₦262,000, profit ₦88,000. Setup planned 5 hours, actual 5 hours 50 minutes.
Pattern 1: every setup ran 15 to 20 percent over plan, mostly on balloon garlands.
Pattern 2: Job 2's quote had no validity date, so the flower price rise came out of her profit.
Tolu adds 20 percent to garland time estimates, starts building garlands the night before, and adds "valid for 7 days" to every quotation.

You do not need many numbers. A few, tracked honestly across every job, tell you whether the business is getting stronger.

**Profit** tells you whether your pricing works. **Setup time accuracy** tells you whether your timelines can be trusted. **Client rating** and **referrals** tell you whether people value your work enough to send others. **Damage and loss** tells you whether your packing and pack-down habits are costing money, since lost rental items are charged to you.

Look at your records every month. If profit per job is falling, check whether material prices have risen faster than your quotes. If setups always run late, build in more buffer or add a helper. If referrals are low despite good ratings, you may simply need to ask for them more directly. Change one habit at a time, then watch the next few jobs to see whether the number moves, so you know which change actually helped.

Keep your receipts with each job record. Photograph market receipts on the day, since paper ones fade and get lost, and save them in the job folder. When you later register your business or open a business account, a few months of tidy records also make it much easier to show what your business earns.

Treat a family job exactly like a paid one. Run the full brief, even with your sister. Agree the design in writing, even if the "approval" is a WhatsApp thumbs-up. Set a ready time and stick to it. Colour
Three colour schemes
One colour in light, medium and dark, plus white. Blush, rose and deep pink for a girl's birthday.
Two or three colours side by side on the wheel. Gold, orange and burnt orange for a traditional wedding.
Two colours opposite on the wheel, one dominant. Royal blue with gold accents for a thanksgiving.
Decor that looks expensive is rarely about money. It is about colour control. A hall with three colours repeated everywhere looks planned. Seven colours look confused.
Monochrome is one colour in light, medium and dark shades, plus white.
Analogous is two or three colours sitting next to each other on the colour wheel, like gold, orange and burnt orange.
Complementary is two colours opposite each other, with one dominant, like royal blue with gold accents. Gold and silver behave like neutrals and suit most schemes.

Clients cannot touch your decor before they book. A good portfolio and clear packages do most of the selling.
When clients ask why they should choose you, answer with facts, not adjectives.
And a 90-day plan turns the skill into steady work.

Worked example
Blessing's planned versus actual
Differences are not failures. They are information.
Quoted 180,000; actual costs 139,000
Setup: 3 hours planned, 3 hours 35 actual
160 balloons planned, 148 used, 9 bursts
Candles switched to flameless
Rated 5 out of 5, cake table bare at the side
For example, Blessing in Benin City decorates her niece's 10th birthday for 45 guests. She quoted 180,000 naira. Actual costs were 139,000, so a paid job would have made 41,000 profit.
She planned 3 hours of setup. It took 3 hours 35 minutes, because the garland took longer than in practice.
She planned 160 balloons, used 148, and had 9 bursts in the afternoon heat.
She switched to flameless candles when she saw the paper backdrop sat close behind the cake table. Safety comes before the plan.

The client rated her 5 out of 5, but said the cake table looked bare from the side. So her reflection names three changes: build garlands the night before, keep 10 percent spare balloons in hot weather, and dress cake tables on all visible sides.
Three packages, inclusions listed
Garland on a backdrop stand, cake table, welcome sign. Up to 50 guests. From 150,000 naira.
Backdrop with drape and garland, cake table, up to 8 guest tables, entrance. From 350,000 naira.
Full hall: stage or high table, backdrop, all tables, chair covers, entrance. Quoted after venue check.
Packages make it easy for clients to choose, and easy for you to quote. These prices are examples only. Build yours from your real costs, then add contingency and profit.
A simple celebration might start from 150,000 naira.
A classic party might start from 350,000.
And a signature event for a full hall is quoted only after a venue check. Always list what is included, so clients compare like with like.

My decor is beautiful, I am reliable, I am affordable. Every decorator says that.
Specific statements, backed by evidence, build trust faster.
For example, Zainab in Kano got a bare question: how much for birthday decoration? She sent her package catalogue, asked three questions, and quoted with photos of similar setups.
She stated her terms: 60 percent deposit, balance three days before. The client booked the same day.
Foundations first, then real jobs
Good goals name a number and a date.
Buy what your records say you rent most
For example, Ifeoma in Owerri spends days 1 to 30 posting her project photos, setting up WhatsApp Business with two packages, and introducing herself to cake makers and a hall manager.
Days 31 to 60, she decorates two paid birthdays and records both.
Days 61 to 90, two more events, including her first church reception. Then she reviews her five numbers.
She saves part of each job's profit for an electric balloon pump, because her records show she rents one every time. Buy by break-even, not by what looks impressive.
Run it like a business
Protect your money and energy
Separate account for business money
Written quotes and deposits, every job
Save towards an equipment fund
Consider CAC business name registration
Rest after big jobs; share the lifting
Open a separate account for business money, so you can see real profit. Keep using written quotations and deposits.
Save part of each job's profit in an equipment fund, so growth is paid for by the business, not borrowed. As work grows, consider registering your business name with the CAC.
And protect your energy. Plan rest after big jobs, share lifting with helpers, and carry water and food.
